It explains the vanished smell and the choice to climb rather than head for the trucks without assuming, as B does, that the monkeyboard was the rig’s highest point or that the air there was clean.

riddle:
Speyside, 2015: the night before the fifty-year-old was bottled, the old cooper tipped one spoonful of clear two-year-old spirit into the vat.
By morning the buyer's lawyers had cancelled the sale.
The cooper was never sacked, and the bottles were later sold labelled only "spirit drink."
The man who caught him in the act simply shook his hand.
chars: Angus, the distillery's elderly cooper; Morag Reid's brother Callum Reid (master blender)
story: The struggling family distillery had been forced to sell its legendary fifty-year-old stock to a conglomerate that planned to rebrand it and shut the site, and the contract required delivery of "Scotch Whisky," so Angus sabotaged it while Callum, who secretly wanted the deal dead, watched and approved. Under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, spirit matured less than three years in oak is not whisky, and any mixture containing even a spoonful of it legally loses the name "whisky" entirely, not just its age statement; the vat became an unsellable "spirit drink," the buyer voided the contract, and the distillery kept its stock and later sold the bottles to collectors as a notorious curiosity.
fact:
INVENTED

Under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, Scotch must be matured in oak for at least three years, but a blend that contains younger spirit is not stripped of the name "whisky." The age statement is simply the youngest component's age, so adding a spoonful of new-make would, at most, change the age statement. It would not mean the vat could no longer be sold as Scotch. The claim that a tiny amount of immature spirit makes the whole mixture legally not whisky is therefore wrong.

(Strictly, though, adding unmatured spirit would make the blend non-compliant, since the regulations require the whole product to have matured for three years. That makes the mixture non-compliant, but it is not a clean rule that it "loses the name" while the rest remains unaffected. The "spirit drink" framing is the right category for noncompliant product, though, so the mechanism is partially right.)
solver:
**Character 1:** The old cooper, who had tended the fifty-year-old cask since he was an apprentice in 1965.

**Character 2:** The distillery owner (occupation: owner and master distiller), who was contractually bound by his creditors to sell that cask to a foreign investor planning to strip the brand.

**Story:** Under Scotch whisky law, spirit must mature at least three years to be called whisky, so one spoonful of two-year-old spirit legally turned the priceless fifty-year-old into mere "spirit drink." The buyer's lawyers voided the contract over the breached "Scotch whisky" specification, and the owner, who had caught the cooper mid-pour but could never have broken the deal himself, shook his hand in thanks.

opus.judge:
A

Story A has the owner himself catch the cooper and shake his hand, which naturally explains why he was never sacked, whereas Story B's master blender merely "watched and approved" and lacks the authority to account for the cooper keeping his job.

B
Story B explains every detail most cleanly: the owner was bound by creditors and could not break the sale himself, so he caught the cooper mid-pour, kept him on and shook his hand. Story A's "watching and approving" blender doesn't fit "caught him in the act," and it doesn't explain who could have sacked the cooper.

sol.judge:
A
Both stories explain why the spoonful killed the sale, but A better explains the handshake and why the cooper kept his job: he freed the owner from a deal the owner couldn’t break himself.

A
Both stories explain the legal downgrade and the handshake, but A also explains why the cooper kept his job and why collectors later bought the bottles as “spirit drink.”

riddle:
Her holds held cod she had no right to catch, yet not one fish went back over the side.
One box in twenty got a different label, and the owner smiled though those boxes would earn him almost nothing.
She steamed past her own company's fish plant to tie up at a busier harbour farther down the coast.
The skipper said the sea had simply been too kind.
chars: Einar, the trawler's owner; Guðrún (trawler skipper)
story: Off the Westfjords, Guðrún's trawler hit such a rich run of cod that it overshot the vessel's remaining cod quota mid-haul, but Iceland's discard ban forbade throwing the surplus back. So she used the little-known "VS-afli" rule of Iceland's fisheries law, which lets a vessel land up to 5% of its catch outside quota on condition that it is sold through a licensed fish auction, with most of the proceeds going to a state fisheries fund. That auction requirement is why she sailed past Einar's own processing plant, which has no fish market, to land at a harbour with an auction hall, and Einar smiled because the over-catch would otherwise have cost him a fine or expensive leased quota.
fact:
REAL

Iceland does have a "VS-afli" (verðmætaskipting/value-shared catch) rule, under which up to 5% of a vessel's catch beyond quota can be landed, must be sold through a fish market (auction), and most proceeds, after costs, go to a state fund (Verkefnasjóður sjávarútvegsins), while the discard ban applies.
solver:
**Character 1:** The trawler *Kari*, a Norwegian fishing vessel ("her").
**Character 2:** Olav, the trawler's skipper (occupation: fishing captain).

**Story:** Targeting haddock, Olav's net came up so full of cod that the catch blew past the *Kari*'s cod quota. Norway's discard ban forbids throwing fish back, so every fish was landed. The over-quota cod, about one box in twenty, was labelled separately to be sold for the fishing authority, with the owner getting only a small handling share. Olav steamed past the company's own small plant to the busy auction harbour with an inspector on hand, where the over-quota catch could be declared legally, and the owner smiled because honest landing meant no fines and the rest of the haul fetched top prices. Asked how they'd broken quota, Olav just shrugged that the sea had been too kind.

opus.judge:
B

Story B ties every detail to one real mechanism: Iceland's VS-afli rule allows exactly 5% (one box in twenty) outside quota, requires auction sale (hence the harbour), and sends most proceeds to a state fund (hence the owner's tiny but fine-avoiding return), whereas Story A's "one in twenty" and harbour choice are merely coincidental.

A
Story A ties every detail to one real mechanism, Iceland's VS-afli rule, which allows exactly 5% (one box in twenty) outside quota with auction-only sales and proceeds mostly to a state fund, whereas Story B makes the one-in-twenty figure a mere coincidence.

sol.judge:
B
The 5% rule explains exactly why one box in twenty was relabelled, and the mandatory auction explains why the skipper bypassed the company plant even though the owner would earn little from those boxes.

A
The 5% rule explains why exactly one box in twenty was marked separately and earned the owner so little, while the mandatory auction explains why the skipper had to bypass the company’s own plant.

riddle: On the eve of the Speyside cask's fiftieth birthday, she refused to wait one more year and ordered it emptied at once. The warehouseman reached for his hydrometer, not his nosing glass. Into the vat she then poured something far younger and far stronger. The bottles of her grandfather's last 1975 filling say only "Aged 12 Years."
chars: Morag Grant, granddaughter of the distillery's founder; Callum Ross (warehouseman at the family's Speyside distillery)
story: Callum's hydrometer showed that the 49-year-old cask had sunk to 40.3% ABV. Under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, nothing below 40% may be sold as Scotch, and in a cool, damp Scottish dunnage warehouse the alcohol evaporates faster than the water, so the strength falls every year rather than rising as it does in Kentucky; one more year would have stripped it of the name, so Morag could not wait for the round-number birthday. To keep a safe margin she vatted it with a 12-year-old cask-strength spirit from the same stills, which kept it a single malt, but the regulations require any age statement to name the youngest whisky in the bottle, so her grandfather's half-century spirit had to be labelled "Aged 12 Years."
fact:
INVENTED

The minimum 40% ABV rule under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 and the youngest-component age-statement rule are real, and in damp, cool warehouses alcohol can evaporate faster than water, so strength falls. But the plan fails on its own terms: blending in a 12-year-old cask-strength spirit would make the result a blended malt (or a vatted malt), not a "single malt", because a single malt must come from one distillery, and the scenario says "same stills," so that part could actually hold. The central mechanism, however, is materially wrong: a cask-strength 12-year-old would raise the ABV, but the age statement would be 12 years, which makes the vatting pointless from a marketing standpoint, and the story's claim that Morag "could not wait" is the weak part. Most importantly, the "single" cask labelled 12 years would have been better left as a 49-year-old at a lower-strength bottling, or reduced or rebottled, since Scotch can't be sold below 40% but can be vatted with a stronger whisky, so the vatting solution is plausible and the regulations are real as described.

Correction: on reflection, the mechanism is REAL.

REAL

The 40% ABV minimum, the falling strength in damp Scottish warehouses, and the youngest-component age-statement rule all exist and work roughly as described.
solver:
**Character 1:** Isla, granddaughter of a late Speyside distiller and now the distillery's owner.

**Character 2:** Angus, the distillery's warehouseman.

**Story:** Angus's hydrometer confirmed Isla's fear: after fifty years of the angels' share, her grandfather's last 1975 cask had sunk to just above 40% ABV, and one more year would drop it below the legal minimum for Scotch whisky. She emptied it at once and married it with a younger, higher-strength 12-year-old spirit to rescue it, and because the law requires the age statement to name the youngest whisky in the bottle, his fifty-year legacy must forever be labelled simply "Aged 12 Years."

opus.judge:
B
Story B covers every detail more fully: it explains the "eve of the fiftieth birthday" timing with a 49-year-old cask, why Scottish warehouse conditions make the strength fall year after year, and why the 12-year-old marriage still yields a single malt labelled by its youngest component.

A
Story A accounts for more of the riddle's odd details: it explains why the strength falls in a Scottish warehouse, keeps the cask correctly at 49 years on the eve of its fiftieth birthday, and keeps the blend a single malt, whereas Story B mislabels the cask's age and skips why the strength drops.

sol.judge:
B
It gets the timing right and connects the hydrometer to the risk of falling below 40% ABV, the stronger 12-year-old whisky to restoring a safe margin, and the youngest whisky in the vat to the label.

A
It explains why the hydrometer mattered, why she emptied the cask before it turned fifty, and why adding stronger 12-year-old whisky protected the blend’s strength but determined its age statement.

riddle:
In Iten at dawn, a stranger stopped the camp's fastest woman just as her group set off on the long run.
He didn't care whether she ran fast or slow. He only cared that she didn't run at all.
She sat on a bench for exactly two hours while her training partners disappeared up the Kerio Valley road.
Then he filled two small tubes, thanked her, and left, and nobody accused her of anything.
chars: Faith Chepkoech; Mr. Otieno (anti-doping control officer)
story: Mr. Otieno arrived unannounced at Faith's Iten camp to draw blood for her Athlete Biological Passport, the long-term profile that flags doping through shifts in her blood markers rather than through any single positive test. Under WADA's blood-collection guidelines, a passport sample may not be taken within two hours of training, because hard exercise shifts plasma volume and distorts haemoglobin and reticulocyte readings, so he made her sit out the long run and wait the full two hours before filling the tubes.
fact:
REAL
WADA's guidelines for blood sample collection for the Athlete Biological Passport do call for the athlete to be seated for at least 10 minutes before sampling and to avoid training for roughly two hours beforehand, since exercise shifts plasma volume and distorts haemoglobin and reticulocyte readings. The "long run" detail is a minor embellishment.
solver:
**Character 1:** Faith, the fastest marathoner at the Iten training camp.

**Character 2 (with occupation):** Mr. Otieno, an anti-doping control officer who arrived unannounced for an out-of-competition blood test for her Athlete Biological Passport.

When the two hours were up, he drew two small vials of blood, thanked her, and drove off, and since it was routine monitoring rather than a suspicion, nobody accused her of anything.

opus.judge:
B

Both stories use the same blood-passport mechanism, but B explicitly accounts for every detail, including the two vials and why nobody accused her (it was routine monitoring rather than suspicion).

A

Story A accounts for every detail: the two-hour no-exercise rule, the two vials, the thanks and departure, and why nobody accused her (routine monitoring, not suspicion), whereas Story B leaves the "two tubes" and "nobody accused her" details unexplained.

sol.judge:
B
It more explicitly accounts for the missed run, the two-hour bench wait, the two tubes, and the lack of any accusation by framing the blood draw as routine monitoring.

A
It explains the two-hour wait and the blood draw while also making clear why no one accused her: it was routine monitoring, not a test prompted by suspicion.

riddle:
For sixty years one cask sat untouched in a damp Speyside warehouse, growing rarer every year.
The night before its record-breaking auction, she drew a sample and handed him a slip reading "39.9."
He wept, though not one drop had spoiled, been stolen or been watered.

chars: Hamish Grant, the distillery's elderly owner; Morag Reid (warehouse manager)

riddle:
On a Permian Basin drilling rig in West Texas, the rotten-egg stink on the floor faded within a minute, and the green hand grinned, "Good, it's gone."
The old hand slammed the alarm instead. He glanced at the orange sock on the mast, then dragged the kid past the shady, sheltered cellar pit and up the sandy rise.
Why did a vanishing smell scare him more than the smell itself?
chars: Cody, a green worker on his first hitch; Earl Haskins (toolpusher)
story: Earl knew the smell was hydrogen sulfide from a sour-gas kick, and that above roughly 100–150 ppm H2S paralyzes the olfactory nerve, so the stink "disappearing" meant the concentration had jumped to a deadly level, not that the leak had stopped. Following the Texas Railroad Commission's H2S rule (Statewide Rule 36), which requires wind indicators and upwind safe-briefing areas, he read the windsock to run upwind, and he skipped the cool cellar for the higher ground because H2S is heavier than air and pools in low spots like cellar pits, where it would have killed them both.
fact:
REAL
H2S does deaden the sense of smell at high concentrations (olfactory fatigue/paralysis begins around 100+ ppm), it is heavier than air and pools in low areas like cellars, and Texas Railroad Commission Statewide Rule 36 does govern H2S operations, including wind direction indicators and safe briefing areas.
solver:
**Character 1:** Danny, a green hand (new roughneck) on his first hitch.
**Character 2:** Earl, a veteran driller (the old hand).

**Story:** Earl knew that hydrogen sulfide smells like rotten eggs only at low levels, and at deadly concentrations it paralyzes your sense of smell within moments, so the stink "fading" meant the gas was getting stronger, not leaving. He hit the alarm, checked the windsock to head crosswind and upwind, and pulled Danny away from the low cellar pit, where the heavier-than-air gas pools, and up the high ground where the air was safe.

opus.judge:
A
Story A covers every detail: olfactory paralysis, the windsock for running upwind, and why the tempting cool cellar was a deadly low spot where heavy H2S pools, with the Texas H2S rule adding grounding; Story B is similar but slightly less complete.

B
Story B explains every clue: the sour-gas kick as the source, olfactory paralysis as the reason the smell vanished, the windsock for choosing an upwind escape, and why the tempting shady cellar was a death trap where the heavy gas would pool.

sol.judge:
A
It more fully explains the old hand’s actions: the fading smell could signal H₂S-induced loss of smell, the windsock showed which way was upwind, and the rise took them away from the cellar where gas could collect.

A
It explains the fading smell, alarm, windsock, and climb away from the sheltered pit without assuming a specific gas kick or treating the loss of smell as proof that the concentration suddenly spiked.

riddle:
In a Ryogoku stable, a healthy 31-year-old finally received the new passport he had waited six years for.
That same week he quit the ring for good, despite going unbeaten in the tournament he had just finished.
His overjoyed master immediately booked a flight to Ulaanbaatar.

chars: Batbayar, a Mongolian-born wrestler who has just become a Japanese citizen; Takeda (sumo stablemaster)
story: Batbayar was born in Mongolia and spent six years naturalizing as a Japanese citizen, because the Japan Sumo Association lets only Japanese nationals buy elder stock (toshiyori kabu) and become coaches. Since 2010, however, the one-foreigner-per-stable rule has counted wrestlers by birthplace rather than passport, so his new citizenship still filled the stable's only foreign slot; he had to retire into his elder post as a suited coach before Takeda could fly to Ulaanbaatar to sign the next Mongolian recruit.
fact:
REAL

The Japan Sumo Association does require elder stock holders to be Japanese nationals, and since 2010 the one-foreign-wrestler-per-stable rule has counted by origin (birthplace) rather than citizenship, so naturalized wrestlers still count as foreign. The details about Batbayar and Takeda are embellishments, but the mechanism holds up.

**Character 2:** Oyakata Tanaka, a sumo stablemaster in Ryogoku.

**Story:** Batbayar waited six years for Japanese citizenship and his new Japanese passport, because only Japanese nationals may become sumo elders. He then retired right after an unbeaten final tournament to become a suited coach at the same stable. With its one-foreigner-per-stable slot now empty, Tanaka joyfully flew to Ulaanbaatar to recruit a new Mongolian prospect.

riddle:
In late 2016, Ammini flew from Dubai to Kochi for her sister's Guruvayur wedding wearing exactly thirty-five grams of the bridal gold, "not one gram more."
Her husband, beside her, wore only one thin chain, though he had paid for half the set.
Her cousin Rani, on the same flight, wore no gold at all, because she had only moved to Dubai that March.
At the Kochi customs desk, the officer weighed Ammini's bangles, checked her passport stamps and waved her through.
chars: Ammini; Rani (nurse at a Dubai hospital)
story: Ammini and Rani were carrying the bride's gold home in pieces on their own bodies to avoid duty, and Rani the nurse worked out the split from India's Baggage Rules, 2016. Those rules allow duty-free jewellery only to a passenger who has lived abroad for over a year, capped at 40 grams and no more than ₹1,00,000 in value for a woman (20 grams and ₹50,000 for a man), so at that winter's price of roughly ₹2,800 per gram, the rupee cap stopped Ammini at 35 grams and her husband at a single chain, while Rani, who had been abroad for less than a year, could carry nothing.
fact:
INVENTED

India's Baggage Rules, 2016 do allow duty-free jewellery for those who have lived abroad over a year, but the caps are 40 g and ₹1,00,000 for women and 20 g and ₹50,000 for men, and the riddle's price of roughly ₹2,800/gram is far off (gold was around ₹2,800/g in about 2010-11, not under the 2016 rules), making the 35-gram rupee-cap arithmetic inconsistent. Also, the claim that Rani, abroad for less than a year, could carry nothing is wrong, since those with under a year abroad have no jewellery allowance but the general ₹15,000 allowance applies to other goods, which is a minor point. The main flaw is that the numbers don't fit the era: at ₹2,800/g, 35 g is about ₹98,000, which fits the cap, but 2016-era prices were about ₹2,800-3,000/g, so this is actually plausible.

Correction: on reflection the arithmetic works, since gold was about ₹2,800-3,000/g in late 2016, and the rules are as described.

REAL
solver:
**Character 1:** Ammini, a Kerala-born woman who has lived in Dubai for several years.

**Character 2:** Mr. Menon, a customs officer at Kochi airport.

**Story:** Indian baggage rules let a woman who has lived abroad for over a year bring in about 40 g of jewellery duty-free, capped at ₹1 lakh in value, which in late 2016 came to roughly 35 g of gold. Her husband's allowance was only ₹50,000 (one thin chain), and Rani's March move meant she had no allowance at all, so Menon weighed the bangles, confirmed Ammini's year abroad from her passport stamps, and waved the bridal gold through duty-free.

It explains the 35-gram cutoff, the husband’s thin chain, Rani’s lack of gold, and the officer’s checks without contradicting the riddle by claiming Rani carried some of the gold.

It explains the 35-gram limit, the husband’s thin chain, and Rani’s ineligibility while also accounting for both customs checks and avoiding B’s contradiction that Rani carried some of the gold.

riddle:
Off Iceland, a trawler hand who has never paid for a drop of diesel scowled when world oil prices spiked mid-trip.
The haul was the same size, and the fish sold for the same price as last time.
The owner, not the crew, paid the fuel bill.
Yet his pay slip came back smaller.
chars: Gunnar, the owner's fleet manager; Jón (deckhand)
story: Jón, like every Icelandic deckhand, is paid not a wage but a share of the catch's sale value (hlutaskipti), and Gunnar's company pays all the fuel. However, the Icelandic fishermen's collective agreement contains a sliding scale that lowers the crew's share percentage whenever the oil price rises relative to catch value, so the mid-trip spike cut Jón's cut of an identical haul.
fact:
REAL

Icelandic fishermen are paid by catch share (hlutaskipti), and the collective agreements do tie the crew's share to the oil price: the "olíuviðmiðun" mechanism lowers the crew's share percentage as fuel costs rise relative to catch value. The details of who pays the fuel and how the scale is applied vary, but the core idea holds roughly as described.
solver:
**Character 1:** Jón, a deckhand on an Icelandic trawler.

**Character 2:** Gunnar, the trawler's owner (a fishing-company boss).

**Story:** Jón is paid not a wage but a share of the catch's value, and under Iceland's crew-share agreement the crew's percentage automatically shrinks when world oil prices climb, because the deal is indexed to fuel costs even though the owner pays the fuel bill. So when oil spiked mid-trip, Gunnar paid for the diesel as always, but the same haul at the same price was split with a smaller crew share, and Jón's pay slip came back lighter.
